q: A small numbered seal on the back of a Spanish bottle states its ageing class and vouches for its origin. Who issues it?
opts: The bodega that made the wine
exp: Every denomination has a Consejo Regulador that writes its rules, inspects its members and numbers each back label. That is why a Spanish ageing term is a checkable claim rather than a marketing word.

q: Ordering the Spanish quality ladder from the loosest rules to the strictest, which sequence is right?
opts: Vino de la Tierra, Vino, DOCa, DO
Vino, DOCa, Vino de la Tierra, DO
Vino, Vino de la Tierra, DO, DOCa
DO, DOCa, Vino, Vino de la Tierra
exp: Each step tightens the permitted grapes, the maximum yields, the ageing minimums and the boundary itself. Vino de Pago sits outside the sequence, since it applies to one estate rather than to a region.

q: An early-ripening black grape with thick skins and modest acidity became the most widely planted red variety in Spain. Which one?
exp: The name comes from temprano, meaning early. Ripening weeks ahead of Garnacha is what lets it succeed at altitude in Ribera del Duero, where autumn arrives without warning.

q: Tinta del Pais, Cencibel and Ull de Llebre all name one variety. Which?
exp: The vine travelled around Spain long before anyone catalogued it, so nearly every region gave it a local name. Tinta de Toro belongs on the same list, as does Portugal's Tinta Roriz.

q: Old bush vines on Priorat slate and the dry pink wines of Navarra both rest on which variety?
exp: Garnacha oxidises easily and can look pale, yet from low-yielding old vines it gives real depth and perfume. Spain, most probably Aragon, is where it came from.

q: A very late-ripening variety that needs real heat to finish gives Jumilla and Yecla their dark, tannic reds. Which is it, and what is it called in France?
opts: Garnacha Tintorera, called Alicante Bouschet in France
exp: Monastrell buds late and ripens very late, so it belongs in the hot southeast. It gives high tannin and dark fruit, and turns meaty and gamey with age.

q: Thick skins and searing acidity let one white variety thrive on a rainy Atlantic coast where rot is the constant threat. Which is it?
exp: Albarino carries the damp of Rias Baixas because its berries are small and its skins tough. Across the Mino in Portugal the same vine is called Alvarinho.

q: A white grape that browns easily in the press house is picked at night under inert gas and finishes with a bitter almond twist. Which one?
exp: Verdejo oxidises readily, so the modern Rueda style depends on night harvesting and protective handling. That faintly bitter, fennel-like finish is its signature.

q: Bodegas in Jerez want a base wine that contributes almost nothing of its own before ageing begins. Which grape gives them that?
exp: Palomino is low in acid, low in aroma and generous in yield. A dry Sherry takes its character from flor, oxygen and wood rather than from fruit, so neutrality is an asset here.

q: Three zones divide the Rioja denomination. Which of them lies in the Basque province of Alava?
exp: Alavesa is the smallest of the three, on chalky clay under the Sierra de Cantabria. Its villages are also the traditional home of the whole-bunch carbonic style drunk within the year.

q: Garnacha ripens most reliably in the warmest, lowest and driest part of Rioja. Which zone is that?
exp: The eastern end lies lower and hotter, with a Mediterranean edge to the climate, and it grows most of the region's Garnacha. It was called Rioja Baja until 2018, an old name that described altitude and not quality.

q: A limestone ridge along Rioja's northern edge blocks the worst of the Atlantic weather. What is it called?
exp: Without that wall the region would be as wet as the Basque coast an hour away. The shelter is what lets Rioja ripen at all at five hundred metres and more.

q: Merchants fleeing a ruined Bordeaux in the nineteenth century brought barrel ageing south to Rioja. What had driven them out?
opts: A French ban on wine exports
A collapse in the price of claret
exp: The louse ruined the French vineyard from the 1860s and reached Rioja only in 1899, some three decades later, and in that gap Rioja learned to age in 225-litre barricas. The habit long outlasted the crisis.

q: A traditional Rioja Gran Reserva smells of coconut, vanilla and dill. Which cellar practice accounts for that?
opts: Long ageing in barrels of American oak
Blending in a share of Moscatel
A month of maceration on the skins
Ageing under a film of flor
exp: American oak is far higher in the lactone that reads as coconut and dill, and Rioja's classic houses have used it for well over a century. French oak gives a tighter, more toasted register.

q: A blender wants floral lift and firm acidity to rescue a soft, broad Tempranillo. Which Rioja variety is reached for?
exp: Graciano yields little and is awkward to grow, which is why it nearly disappeared, but a few percent transforms a blend with violet aromatics and bite.

q: One variety supplies both the backbone of white Rioja and a third of the classic Cava blend. Which is it?
opts: Viura, known in Catalonia as Macabeo
Verdejo, known in Catalonia as Subirat Parent
Malvasia, known in Catalonia as Parellada
Garnacha Blanca, known in Catalonia as Xarel-lo
exp: Viura and Macabeo are one grape under two names. It is neutral and high in acid, which suits both a barrel-aged white Rioja and a bottle of sparkling wine.
